title: Smart Lighting Application for Energy Saving and User Well-Being in the Residential Environment
review_question: To provide an overview of smart lighting systems' effect on energy and well-being in the residential environment.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Studies published from 2001 onwards, peer-reviewed journal articles and reviews, English language. Excluded: irrelevant subject areas (material, economy, agriculture, earth/planetary, arts, pharmacology, chemistry, chemical engineering, bionic, immunology, business), non-residential environments, conceptual frameworks without energy/well-being outcomes, non-smart systems, algorithms exclusively, user interaction only, specific user groups (e.g., severe dementia), technical papers, or full papers not available. References of included papers were also screened.

findings.antecedent: Smart lighting systems (various light sources, communication protocols, control inputs, sensors, algorithms) in residential environments
findings.quote: The energy savings percentages range from 2 to 93%

findings.antecedent: Commercially available smart LED bulbs (in standby mode)
findings.quote: Their results showed a standby consumption of (less than) 0.5 W per bulb.

findings.antecedent: Smart lighting systems (various light sources, communication protocols, control inputs, sensors, algorithms) in residential environments
findings.consequent: User well-being and comfort (visual comfort, satisfaction, health, emotion, performance, circadian rhythm synchronization)
findings.quote: nine studies included well-being outcomes... None of the studies was able to draw firm conclusions

synthesis_conclusions: There is a need for an unambiguous definition of a 'smart lighting system' and its required components to facilitate research comparison and reduce confusion.

Clear documentation of smart lighting system components (light sources, communication protocols, control inputs, sensor types, and algorithms) is essential for assessing system quality and performance.
For studies involving daylight, fundamental documentation of geographical study location, date, and time of execution is required.
High-quality (controlled) intervention studies on human performance and interaction measures are needed to corroborate light effects beyond vision in residential environments.
Studies focusing on user acceptance and interactions with smart lighting systems are needed to inform optimal design and integration into residential settings.
evidence_gaps: Lack of an unambiguous definition and extensive characterization of 'smart lighting system' components.
Limited exploration of smart lighting systems' effects on well-being and energy performance in residential environments.
Insufficient high-quality intervention studies on human performance and interaction measures related to smart lighting in residential settings.
Lack of studies focusing on user acceptance and interactions with smart lighting technology in homes.
Study durations for well-being outcomes (e.g., sleep quality) are often too short to capture long-term effects.
Limited focus on component-level performance beyond standby power consumption.
Incomplete documentation of instrumentalism for light measurements and completeness of energy saving potential calculations.

moderators.effect: Influences the energy saving potential of smart lighting systems, with studies closer to the equator potentially showing higher savings.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Studies near the equator (Malaysia, ~3° N) reported 55% energy saving, while studies further north (South Korea, ~37° N) reported lower savings (2%).

limitations: Difficulty in comparing studies due to varying definitions of 'smart lighting' and required system components.
The broadness of 'energy' and 'well-being' as research areas made it challenging to find specific relevant papers.
Exclusion of conference contributions, which might have covered ongoing initiatives or prototypes.
The search strategy primarily focused on complete smart lighting systems, with limited focus on specific components like communication protocols or occupancy sensors.

Limited documentation of general study characteristics and lighting system specifics (e.g., instrumentalism for light measurements, completeness of energy saving calculations) in the included studies.
The literature search was conducted using only two databases (Scopus and Web of Science), potentially limiting the breadth of results.

paper_metadata.crossref_title: Smart Lighting Application for Energy Saving and User Well-Being in the Residential Environment
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The idea of smart lighting has emerged over the years in commercial and industrial environments, with a focus on energy saving. With the advancement in technology, smart lighting can now offer opportunities in addition to energy saving to users in home environments for the provision of a comfortable atmosphere and the maintenance of user well-being. Currently, research in the smart lighting field is predominantly dedicated to energy saving in non-residential environments; meanwhile, the residential environments have not been explored. Therefore, a literature review was conducted to provide an overview of smart lighting systems’ effect on energy and well-being in the residential environment. Current research is mostly limited to designing and developing a smart lighting system in a controlled environment, with a limited evaluation of well-being and comfort. The review shows that residential smart lighting application possibilities and opportunities are not widely and thoroughly explored.
